mainTopic: Personal requests in תפלה, and the festivals of the גוים
overview: This עמוד finishes the מחלוקת between רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע about where a person asks for his own needs in תפלה. The חכמים say these requests go in שומע תפלה, and שמואל rules that way. Three אמוראים then add more room: a fitting request at the end of each ברכה, a prayer for the sick or for a livelihood in the matching ברכה, and long requests after the תפלה. A new משנה lists the festivals of the גוים, and the חכמים limit which death-days count. It also teaches that private celebrations forbid business only on that day and only with that man. The גמרא dates קלנדא and סטרנורא and tells how אדם הראשון first fasted over the shrinking winter days and then celebrated when they grew longer. A similar story about his first night ends with the one-horned bull he offered. Next, the גמרא rules like רבי יוחנן: קלנדא forbids business only with the people who celebrate it, as shown from a ברייתא and from the משנה's words 'that man'. Finally, רבי ישמעאל teaches that Jews at a גוי's feast for his son are guilty from the moment of the invitation, and the rule that follows from this continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: The root of the dispute: do we learn from משה?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע learns from משה that praise comes first and requests come after. רבי אליעזר says משה was special, so we cannot copy him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע holds that we learn from משה. רבי אליעזר holds that we do not learn from משה, because משה is different: he was a man of great spiritual strength.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבי יהושע and רבי אליעזר disagree about where personal requests go. It all depends on whether משה's way of praying is a model for everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה first praised ה׳ and only then asked to enter the land, so רבי יהושע says everyone should praise first and ask afterward. רבי אליעזר answers that משה was on a level where he knew how to pray in that order. Regular people should not copy him, so they may ask for their needs first.

keyTerms.meaning: his strength is great; he was a person of great stature
he holds / he is of the opinion

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua holds: we learn from Moshe,
phrases.notes: Think of how משה prayed in דברים 3:23-25: he praised ה׳ first, and only then asked for what he wanted.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר סָבַר: לָא יָלְפִינַן מִמֹּשֶׁה,
phrases.english: and Rabbi Eliezer holds: we do not learn from Moshe,
Moshe is different, because his strength was great.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the רבי אליעזר / רבי יהושע dispute from the earlier ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the basis of the disagreement between רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree about whether משה's order of praying (praise first, then requests) is a model for everyone.

steps.title: The חכמים: personal requests go in שומע תפלה
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים reject both views. A person asks for his needs inside the ברכה of שומע תפלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים say: the law follows neither this one nor that one. Rather, a person asks for his needs in the blessing of 'Who hears prayer.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a third opinion. The חכמים say personal requests belong neither before nor after the whole תפלה, but inside it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר put requests before the תפלה, and רבי יהושע put them after. The חכמים place them in the middle, in the ברכה of שומע תפלה, the general ברכה asking ה׳ to accept our prayers.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Who hears prayer': the last of the request ברכות in שמונה עשרה

phrases.english: And the Sages say:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא כְּדִבְרֵי זֶה וְלֹא כְּדִבְרֵי זֶה,
phrases.english: not like the words of this one, and not like the words of that one,
rather, a person asks for his needs
in 'Who hears prayer.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: לֹא כְּדִבְרֵי זֶה וְלֹא כְּדִבְרֵי זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a third position, rejecting both רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Personal requests are said within the ברכה of שומע תפלה.

steps.title: שמואל rules like the חכמים
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes שמואל: the הלכה is that personal requests are said in שומע תפלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: The law is that a person asks for his needs in 'Who hears prayer.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the practical ruling. The הלכה follows the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Of the three views, שמואל decides for the חכמים. Personal requests have a proper home inside שמונה עשרה, in שומע תפלה. The next steps build on this ruling.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basic rule that the following אמוראים expand on with their 'אף על פי' additions.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל, הֲלָכָה:
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: the law is:
a person asks for his needs in 'Who hears prayer.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל, הֲלָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the הלכה in favor of the חכמים from the previous step.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה is that personal requests are said in שומע תפלה.

steps.title: A fitting request may be added at the end of each ברכה
steps.stepSummary: In the name of רב: even though requests belong in שומע תפלה, a person may add a matching request at the end of each ברכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה בריה דרב שמואל בר שילת said in the name of רב: Even though they said that a person asks for his needs in 'Who hears prayer,' if he wants to say, at the end of each blessing, something that matches that blessing, he may say it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds flexibility to the ruling. שומע תפלה is not the only place for personal requests.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'אף על פי' tell us the basic rule still stands, but it is not exclusive. A person may add his own words at the end of any ברכה, as long as they fit the theme of that ברכה.

keyTerms.meaning: similar to / matching the theme of

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר שִׁילַת מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב:
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat said in the name of Rav:
Even though they said
that a person asks for his needs in 'Who hears prayer,'
but if he wants to say
at the end of each and every blessing
something that matches each and every blessing,
phrases.notes: He means a personal request that fits the topic of that particular ברכה.

phrases.english: he may say it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמְרוּ שׁוֹאֵל אָדָם צְרָכָיו בְּשׁוֹמֵעַ תְּפִלָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the ruling of step 3 by allowing requests in other ברכות too.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person may add a personal request matching each ברכה at its end.

steps.title: Praying for a sick person or a livelihood in the matching ברכה
steps.stepSummary: Also in the name of רב: a person with a sick family member prays for him in the ברכה for the sick, and someone who needs a livelihood asks in ברכת השנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר אשי said in the name of רב: Even though they said that a person asks for his needs in 'Who hears prayer,' if he has a sick person in his house, he says it in the blessing for the sick. And if he needs a livelihood, he says it in the blessing of the years.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives concrete examples of adding a personal request in the ברכה that matches it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows the earlier idea in action. A request for a sick person fits naturally in רפאנו, and a request for income fits in ברך עלינו. The general rule of שומע תפלה does not block these.

keyTerms.meaning: the ברכה of the years, for a good year and livelihood (ברך עלינו)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi said in the name of Rav:
Even though they said
that a person asks for his needs in 'Who hears prayer,'

phrases.aramaic: אִם יֵשׁ לוֹ חוֹלֶה בְּתוֹךְ בֵּיתוֹ
phrases.english: if he has a sick person in his house,
he says it in the blessing for the sick,
and if he needs a livelihood,
he says it in the blessing of the years.
phrases.notes: That is the ברכה of ברך עלינו.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives specific examples of the matching-ברכה idea from step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Requests for a sick person go in ברכת חולים, and requests for livelihood go in ברכת השנים.

steps.title: Long personal prayers after finishing שמונה עשרה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי: after finishing his תפלה, a person may add requests, even as long as the וידוי of יום הכפורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: Even though they said that a person asks for his needs in 'Who hears prayer,' if he wants to say them after his prayer, even as long as the order of יום הכפורים, he may say them.
steps.whatsHappening: A third אמורא adds one more allowance. After finishing שמונה עשרה, there is no limit on how much a person may ask.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Inside the תפלה, requests are limited to fitting places. Once the תפלה is over, a person may pour out his heart at any length, even as long as the prayers of יום הכפורים.

keyTerms.meaning: like the order (of prayers) of Yom Kippur

steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה follows the חכמים: personal requests go in שומע תפלה. A person may also add fitting requests in each ברכה, such as for the sick or for a livelihood. After the תפלה, he may add as much as he wants.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
Even though they said
that a person asks for his needs in 'Who hears prayer,'

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אִם בָּא לוֹמַר אַחַר תְּפִלָּתוֹ,
phrases.english: but if he wants to say them after his prayer,
even as long as the order of Yom Kippur,
phrases.notes: He means the very long confession prayers said on Yom Kippur.

phrases.english: he may say them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further allowance after the תפלה, alongside the allowances inside the תפלה from steps 4-5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After finishing the תפלה, a person may add personal requests of any length.

steps.title: רבי מאיר lists the festivals of the גוים
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה opens with רבי מאיר's list of the festivals of the גוים.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the festivals of the גוים: קלנדא, סטרנורא, קרטסים, the festival day of their kings, the king's birthday, and the day of the king's death. This is the view of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It names the festivals of the גוים, on which the earlier rules about doing business with them apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list has two groups: fixed public festivals (קלנדא, סטרנורא, קרטסים) and days tied to the king. רבי מאיר counts the king's death-day as a festival with no conditions. The חכמים will disagree on that point next.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה (the core text the גמרא discusses)
A festival day of the kings

phrases.english: MISHNA: And these are the festivals of gentiles
Kalenda, Saturnalia, and Kratesis
and the day of the festival of their kings
and the day of birth, and the day of death
phrases.notes: He means the king's birthday and the day the king died.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Meir

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה defining which days count as festivals of the גוים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי מאיר, the festivals are קלנדא, סטרנורא, קרטסים, the kings' festival day, the king's birthday, and the king's death-day.

steps.title: The חכמים limit which death-days count
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say a death-day counts only if it includes burning, because only then is it connected to עבודה זרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים say: any death that has burning connected to it has עבודה זרה in it. A death without burning has no עבודה זרה in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים disagree with רבי מאיר about the king's death-day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר counted every king's death-day. The חכמים make it depend on whether there was burning, since a death with burning involves עבודה זרה and a death without burning does not.

keyTerms.meaning: Burning (here, a public burning at the king's death)

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say
any death that includes burning
includes idol worship
and one that does not include burning
does not include idol worship

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי מאיר's item 'the day of death'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A death-day counts as a festival only when burning is part of it.

steps.title: Private celebrations forbid only that day and that person
steps.stepSummary: Personal celebrations of a single גוי forbid business only on that day and only with that person.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the day a גוי shaves his beard and his locks, the day he came up from the sea, the day he left prison, and a גוי who made a feast for his son: it is forbidden only on that day and only with that man.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a second kind of celebration: personal events of one גוי. Their prohibition is much narrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Public festivals affect all גוים, but a private celebration matters only to the person celebrating. So the prohibition covers only that day and that man, and other גוים are permitted.
steps.whatToRemember: Public festivals are a broad category. Private celebrations forbid only that day and that one person.

phrases.english: But the day of shaving his beard and his locks
and the day on which he came up from the sea
and the day he left prison
and a gentile who made a feast for his son
it is forbidden only on that day
and with that man alone

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts the public festivals with private celebrations.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For private celebrations, the prohibition applies only on that day and only with that person.

steps.title: When קלנדא and סטרנורא fall
steps.stepSummary: רב חנן בר רבא dates קלנדא to the eight days after the winter תקופה and סטרנורא to the eight days before it, and he gives a memory aid from a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנן בר רבא said: קלנדא is the eight days after the winter solstice, and סטרנורא is the eight days before it. Your memory aid is 'behind and before You have hemmed me in.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by explaining when the first two festivals in the משנה take place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists קלנדא first even though it comes after the solstice. The פסוק also says 'behind' (after) before 'before'. This helps you remember that the first-listed festival, קלנדא, is the one after the solstice.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
Season change, here the winter solstice

steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume the list is in calendar order. קלנדא is listed first but comes after סטרנורא.

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָ׳ אָמַר רַב חָנָן בַּר רָבָא
phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav Ḥanan bar Rava says
Kalenda is eight days after the solstice
Saturnalia is eight days before the solstice
and your mnemonic: "Behind and before You have hemmed me in, etc."
phrases.notes: תהלים 139:5. 'Behind' comes first, just as the after-solstice festival is named first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the dates of the first two festivals in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קלנדא is the 8 days after the winter solstice, and סטרנורא is the 8 days before it.

steps.title: אדם הראשון fears the shrinking days
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells how אדם הראשון saw the days getting shorter, feared it was his punishment, and fasted for eight days.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: when אדם הראשון saw the day getting shorter and shorter, he said, 'Woe is me! Maybe because I sinned, the world is growing dark around me and going back to chaos. This must be the death decreed on me from Heaven.' So he sat for eight days fasting and praying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to explain where these two eight-day festivals came from. This first part covers the eight days before the solstice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אדם did not yet know that days naturally get shorter in winter. He thought it was the death punishment for his sin. His eight days of fasting line up with the eight days of סטרנורא before the solstice.

keyTerms.meaning: Chaos and emptiness, as before creation

phrases.english: The Sages taught
when Adam the first man saw
the day getting progressively shorter
he said: Woe is me!
perhaps because I sinned
the world is growing dark around me
and returning to chaos and emptiness

phrases.aramaic: וְזוֹ הִיא מִיתָה שֶׁנִּקְנְסָה עָלַי מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם
phrases.english: and this is the death decreed upon me from Heaven
he arose and sat eight days in fasting and in prayer
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets, 'and in prayer,' appear in some versions and not others.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן לְפִי שֶׁרָאָה אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the background to the eight days before the solstice described in step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אדם fasted for the eight days before the solstice, fearing that the shortening days were his punishment.

steps.title: אדם הראשון celebrates the lengthening days
steps.stepSummary: When the days began to lengthen after the solstice, אדם realized this was nature and made eight days of celebration. The next year he celebrated all sixteen days.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he saw the season of טבת and saw the day getting longer, he said, 'This is just the way the world works.' He went and made eight festive days. The next year he made both sets of eight days into festive days.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and explains the eight days after the solstice, which match קלנדא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once אדם saw the days lengthening, he understood it was nature and not a punishment. He celebrated the eight days after the solstice. A year later he turned the fasting days into festive days too, which gives both eight-day periods.

keyTerms.meaning: The season of טבת, the winter solstice
The natural way of the world

phrases.english: once he saw the season of Tevet
and saw the day getting progressively longer
he said: This is the way of the world
he went and made eight festive days
the following year
he made both these and those into festive days
phrases.notes: 'These and those' means the eight fasting days and the eight celebration days.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story and explains the eight days after the solstice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אדם celebrated eight days after the solstice, and the next year he celebrated both eight-day periods.

steps.title: אדם's intention versus the גוים' intention
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by contrasting אדם, who set the days לשם שמים, with the גוים, who set them for עבודה זרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He set them up for the sake of Heaven, and they set them up for the sake of idol worship.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא closes by explaining how holy days of אדם became the festivals of the גוים listed in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The days began as אדם's thanks to הקב״ה. Later גוים kept the same dates but used them for עבודה זרה. That is why the משנה treats them as forbidden festivals.
steps.whatToRemember: קלנדא and סטרנורא come from אדם הראשון's fasting and celebration around the winter solstice. He meant them for הקב״ה, but the גוים turned them into days of עבודה זרה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a festival's status comes from how it is used now. The same dates became עבודה זרה festivals because of the גוים' intention.

phrases.english: He established them for the sake of Heaven
and they established them for the sake of idol worship

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the lesson of the story and connects it back to the festivals in the משנה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: אדם set up these days לשם שמים, but the גוים adopted them for עבודה זרה, which is why they are festivals of the גוים.

steps.title: How could אדם fear short days if the world was created in ניסן?
steps.stepSummary: The story of אדם fits the view that the world was created in תשרי, but it seems not to fit the view that it was created in ניסן.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense if the world was created in תשרי, because אדם saw short days and had not yet seen long days. But if the world was created in ניסן, he had already seen both short days and long days.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the story of אדם fasting over the shrinking days. According to the opinion that the world was created in ניסן, he should already have known how the seasons work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If creation was in תשרי, אדם's first months were all shrinking days, so his fear was natural. If creation was in ניסן, he lived through the spring and the summer, when days grow longer, and then the fall, when they get shorter. He would already have known that days go up and down, so why would he be afraid?

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense / granted (opens a 'this fits, but that doesn't' challenge)
According to the one who says

phrases.english: It makes sense according to the one who says:
"The world was created in תשרי,"
phrases.notes: תשרי is in the fall, so from creation onward the days kept getting shorter.

phrases.english: he saw short days,
he had not yet seen long days.
But according to the one who says:
"The world was created in ניסן,"

phrases.aramaic: הָא חֲזָא לֵיהּ יוֹמֵי זוּטֵי וְיוֹמֵי אֲרִיכֵי!
phrases.english: he had already seen short days and long days!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר בְּתִשְׁרִי נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the story of אדם's eight-day fast told in Steps 11 to 13
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא that אדם feared the shortening days were his punishment
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If creation was in ניסן, אדם had already seen the days lengthen and shorten, so the shortening should not have scared him

steps.title: He had never seen days this short
steps.stepSummary: אדם had seen short days, but never days as short as the ones just before the winter solstice.
steps.simpleTranslation: He had not seen days that were this short.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Even under the ניסן view, אדם had never seen days as short as those right before winter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer changes what frightened אדם. It was not that days got shorter. It was how extremely short they became. Days shorter than anything he had seen before made him think something was wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: This much / to such an extent

phrases.english: Short days to this extent he had not seen.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets. The meaning stays the same.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 14
steps.terutzResolutionType: Clarifies the cause of the fear: the degree of shortness, not the shortening itself
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under the ניסן view, אדם had seen short days and should not have been afraid
steps.terutzMaskana: He had never seen days as short as those before the winter solstice, so his fear still makes sense
steps.whatToRemember: The story of אדם fits both views of when the world was created. What scared him was days shorter than any he had ever seen.

steps.title: אדם's terror at the first sunset
steps.stepSummary: On the day he was created, אדם saw the sun set and thought the world was going dark because of his sin. He fasted and cried all night, and חוה cried with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: On the day אדם הראשון was created, when the sun set on him, he said: Woe is me! Because I sinned, the world is growing dark around me and will go back to emptiness and chaos. This is the death that Heaven decreed on me. He sat fasting and crying all night, and חוה cried opposite him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא with a similar story about אדם. This one is about his very first night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story is built like the solstice story. אדם sees darkness, thinks it is his punishment, and fasts. Here it happens on a smaller scale, with one night instead of a whole season. He believed the darkness was the death he had been warned about.

keyTerms.meaning: Emptiness and chaos, the state before creation

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
On the day that אדם הראשון was created,
once the sun set on him,
he said: Woe is me,
for because I sinned
the world is going dark around me,
and the world will return to emptiness and chaos,

phrases.aramaic: וְזוֹ הִיא מִיתָה שֶׁנִּקְנְסָה עָלַי מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם.
phrases.english: and this is the death that was decreed on me from Heaven.

phrases.aramaic: הָיָה יוֹשֵׁב בְּתַעֲנִית וּבוֹכֶה כׇּל הַלַּיְלָה,
phrases.english: He sat fasting and crying the whole night,
and חוה was crying opposite him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן יוֹם שֶׁנִּבְרָא בּוֹ אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a second, similar ברייתא about אדם mistaking nature for punishment
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אדם thought the first nightfall was his death sentence for sinning, and he fasted and cried all night

steps.title: At dawn אדם understands and brings an offering
steps.stepSummary: When dawn came, אדם realized night is part of nature. He offered a bull whose horns came before its hooves, based on a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: When dawn rose, he said: This is the natural way of the world. He got up and offered a bull whose horns came before its hooves, as it says: "It will please ה׳ more than a bull, an ox with horns and hooves."
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes the story. At sunrise אדם relaxes, and he thanks ה׳ with a special offering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says this bull's horns 'came before' its hooves. It learns this from the פסוק, which lists horns (מקרן) before hooves (מפריס). Once אדם saw that night is part of nature, his fear turned into thanks, and he brought an offering.

keyTerms.meaning: The natural way of the world

phrases.english: Once dawn rose,
he said: This is the natural way of the world.
He got up and offered a bull
whose horns came before its hooves,
as it says: "And it will please ה׳ more than an ox,
a bull with horns and hooves."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story begun in Step 16
steps.mimraCoreRuling: At dawn אדם understood that night is natural, and he offered a bull whose horns came before its hooves

steps.title: שמואל: אדם's bull had one horn
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה reports in the name of שמואל that the bull אדם offered had a single horn in its forehead, based on the same פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: The bull that אדם הראשון offered had one horn in its forehead, as it says: "It will please ה׳ more than an ox, a bull with horns and hooves."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another detail about אדם's bull. It had only one horn, in the middle of its forehead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל reads the same פסוק to learn something new about the bull. The word for 'horns' in the פסוק is the source, and the next step shows exactly how he reads it.

phrases.english: And רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל:
The bull that אדם הראשון offered
had one horn in its forehead,
as it says: "And it will please ה׳ more than an ox,
a bull with horns and hooves."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל שׁוֹר שֶׁהִקְרִיב אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another detail about the bull from Step 17, using the same פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אדם's bull had a single horn in its forehead

steps.title: The word 'horns' sounds like two
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that מקרין means horns in the plural, so the bull had two horns.
steps.simpleTranslation: But מקרין means two horns!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל. The word in the פסוק sounds plural, which means more than one horn.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is about how the word is read. If the word is pronounced מקרין, it suggests horns, more than one. That goes against שמואל's claim of a single horn.

phrases.english: "Makrin" means two!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's reading of the פסוק in Step 18
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's claim that the bull had one horn
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word in the פסוק sounds plural, so it points to two horns, not one

steps.title: The spelling shows one horn
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that the word is written מקרן, without a י, which hints at a single horn.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: It is written מקרן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends שמואל. It points to the way the word is spelled, not the way it is pronounced.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word is spelled without the י that makes it sound plural, so it can be read as 'a horn.' The spelling supports one horn.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written (refers to the spelling in the פסוק)

phrases.english: רב נחמן בר יצחק said:
"Makran" is written.
phrases.notes: The word is spelled without a י, so it can be read as 'a horn,' just one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק מַקְרָן כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading from the spelling instead of the pronunciation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The plural sound of the word means two horns
steps.terutzMaskana: The spelling without a yud supports a single horn

steps.title: Does Rome's קלנדא forbid business with the towns it rules?
steps.stepSummary: רב מתנה asks whether the towns under Roman rule are included in the ban on business on קלנדא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מתנה said: רומי celebrates קלנדא, and all the nearby towns are ruled by it. Are those towns forbidden or permitted?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the הלכה of the festivals of the גוים. It asks whether a ruling city's festival forbids business with the towns under its rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The towns do not celebrate קלנדא themselves, but they serve רומי and pay it taxes. The question is whether this connection is enough to forbid doing business with them during קלנדא.

phrases.english: רב מתנה said:
רומי, which celebrates קלנדא,
and all the towns near it
are ruled by it,
are those towns forbidden or permitted?
phrases.notes: He is asking about doing business with the people of those towns during קלנדא.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מַתְנָה רוֹמִי שֶׁעָשְׂתָה קָלֶנְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back from the story about אדם to the halacha of קלנדא
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the business ban of קלנדא also covers the towns ruled by רומי that do not celebrate it

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי vs. רבי יוחנן on קלנדא
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי says קלנדא forbids business with everyone. רבי יוחנן says it forbids business only with those who worship on it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: קלנדא is forbidden for everyone. רבי יוחנן said: It is forbidden only with those who worship on it.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer רב מתנה's question in different ways.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן לוי treats קלנדא as a festival so widespread that it forbids business with all גוים, including the nearby towns. רבי יוחנן limits the ban to people who actually celebrate it, so towns that only serve רומי are permitted.

phrases.english: רבי יהושע בן לוי said:
קלנדא is forbidden with everyone,
רבי יוחנן said:
It is forbidden only with its worshippers.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי אָמַר קָלֶנְדָּא אֲסוּרָה לַכֹּל הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב מתנה's question with a disagreement
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהושע בן לוי: forbidden with everyone. רבי יוחנן: forbidden only with those who celebrate it
steps.whyThisMatters: This disagreement decides whether a festival's ban follows the people who are connected to the celebrating power or only the people who actually take part.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבי יוחנן on קלנדא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that even though Rome set up קלנדא and the nearby towns are under Rome's rule, the ban applies only to those who worship on it. This matches רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא was taught that agrees with רבי יוחנן: Even though Rome made קלנדא, and all the towns near it are ruled by it, קלנדא itself is forbidden only with its worshippers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up רבי יוחנן's opinion from the previous step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might have thought that towns under Roman rule count as part of Rome's festival. The ברייתא says no: being ruled by Rome does not make someone a worshipper. So business is forbidden only with people who actually celebrate קלנדא, which is exactly רבי יוחנן's view.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא was taught that agrees with him
Are ruled by, are under the control of
Its worshippers, the people who celebrate it

steps.whyThisMatters: It settles the question רב מתנה asked in Step 21. Towns that are merely ruled by Rome are not included in the ban.

phrases.english: It was taught in a ברייתא in agreement with רבי יוחנן:
Even though they said
that Rome established קלנדא,

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל עֲיָירוֹת הַסְּמוּכוֹת לָהּ מִשְׁתַּעְבְּדוֹת לָהּ,
phrases.english: and all the towns near it are ruled by it,
it itself is not forbidden
phrases.notes: "It" here is the festival of קלנדא. Doing business on it is not forbidden in general.

phrases.english: except with its worshippers alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא supporting the second opinion (רבי יוחנן) in Step 22.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's view that קלנדא forbids business only with those who worship on it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא stating that even the towns ruled by Rome are not included; only worshippers are.

steps.title: The ברייתא continues: time limits for other festivals
steps.stepSummary: The same ברייתא lists more festivals (סטרנליא, קרטסים, the kings' festival, coronation day). Before them business is forbidden and after them it is allowed. A private feast for a son is forbidden only on that day and only with that man.
steps.simpleTranslation: סטרנליא and קרטסים, the festival day of their kings, and the day a king was crowned: before them it is forbidden, after them it is allowed. A non-Jew who made a feast for his son: it is forbidden only on that day and only with that man.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps going and gives rules for a few more holidays. It also covers a private family celebration.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Public national festivals have a ban that starts before the day but ends once the day is over. A private celebration is limited in two ways. It covers only the day itself, and only the man who is celebrating.

keyTerms.meaning: A festival day of the kings

steps.confusionAlert: 'Before it forbidden, after it allowed' is about the public festivals only. The son's feast has a stricter limit: only the day itself.

phrases.english: Saturnalia and Kratesis,
and the festival day of their kings,
and the day on which a king was crowned:
before it, forbidden; after it, permitted.
And a non-Jew who made a feast for his son:
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word בּוֹ in round brackets and some leave it out. The meaning stays the same either way.

phrases.english: it is forbidden only on that day
and with that man.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the text of the same ברייתא quoted in Step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Public festivals: forbidden before, permitted after. A private feast for a son: forbidden only that day and only with that man.

steps.title: רב אשי: our משנה teaches this too
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says our own משנה also supports רבי יוחנן. He quotes its list of private celebrations, which are forbidden only on that day and with that man.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: We also learned this in our משנה, which teaches: the day he shaves his beard and his locks, the day he came up from the sea, and the day he left prison: it is forbidden only on that day and with that man.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי announces a second proof for רבי יוחנן, this time from our משנה. He quotes the words he will use. This step sets up the reasoning that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the support came from a ברייתא. Now רב אשי wants a source with even more weight, the משנה itself. The key words are 'that man'. In the next step he explains why those words prove רבי יוחנן's point.

keyTerms.meaning: We too have learned it (in our משנה)

phrases.english: רב אשי said:
We too have also learned this,
as it teaches:
the day of shaving his beard and his locks,
and the day on which he came up from the sea,
and the day on which he left prison:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין אָסוּר אֶלָּא אוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם בִּלְבַד
phrases.english: it is forbidden only on that day alone
and with that man.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second source, the משנה, after the ברייתא's support.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's view that the ban applies only to those who celebrate.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's words 'only that day and that man' about private celebrations.

steps.title: 'That man' excludes the people he rules
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains the proof. 'That day' excludes the days before and after. 'That man' must exclude the people ruled by him, which shows the ban does not reach those under someone's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that 'that day' comes to exclude the days before and after. But 'that man', what does it come to exclude? Doesn't it come to exclude the people ruled by him? Learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי shows why the משנה's wording proves רבי יוחנן right. The גמרא then accepts the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every word in the משנה should teach something. 'That day' clearly teaches that the days before and after are allowed. 'That man' must also teach something. It teaches that the people under his rule are not included, just like the towns under Rome are not included in קלנדא.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense / granted (sets up a contrast)
Learn from this; the proof is accepted

steps.whatToRemember: The final view follows רבי יוחנן. A festival bans business only with the people who actually celebrate it, not with those who are merely ruled by the celebrants. Support comes from a ברייתא and from the משנה's words 'that man'.
steps.confusionAlert: 'That man' does not just mean 'not other non-Jews in general'. That would be obvious for a private party. The extra point is that even the people under his rule are not included.

phrases.english: It makes sense that "that day"
comes to exclude before it and after it,
but "that man"
comes to exclude what?
Is it not to exclude those ruled by him?
Learn from this.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא אוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם לְאַפּוֹקֵי לְפָנָיו וּלְאַחֲרָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the משנה quoted in Step 25 proves רבי יוחנן's view, and closes the topic.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's view that those merely ruled by the celebrants are not included in the ban.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's extra phrase 'that man', which must be there to exclude those ruled by him.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ban applies only to the celebrants themselves, not to those under their rule, as רבי יוחנן said.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל: Jews at a non-Jew's feast are treated as eating idol offerings
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי ישמעאל. Jews outside ארץ ישראל are innocently involved in עבודה זרה. When a non-Jew makes a feast for his son and invites them, the פסוק treats them as if they ate idol offerings, even if they eat their own food.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי ישמעאל says that Jews living outside the Land are idol worshippers 'in purity', meaning without realizing it. How? A non-Jew makes a feast for his son and invites all the Jews in his town. They eat their own food, drink their own drinks, and have their own waiter serving them. Even so, the פסוק counts it as if they ate from offerings to the dead, as it says: 'and he will call you, and you will eat of his sacrifice.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about a non-Jew's feast for his son. It says that the Jewish guests carry guilt even though they eat only kosher food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier steps already counted a private feast for a son as a celebration of the non-Jew. This ברייתא adds something new: simply being at such a feast is treated as taking part in the idol offerings. The guests' food does not matter. Joining the event is the problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'in purity'; here it means innocently, without meaning to
Offerings to the dead, meaning offerings to idols

steps.confusionAlert: 'בטהרה' does not mean the Jews are doing something pure or allowed. It means they are involved in עבודה זרה without realizing it.

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Yishmael says:
Jews who live outside the Land of Israel
are idol worshippers 'in purity',
phrases.notes: He means they are doing it innocently, without even realizing it.

phrases.english: How so?
A non-Jew who made a feast for his son
and invited all the Jews in his town,
even though they eat their own food
and drink their own drinks,
and their own waiter stands and serves them,
the verse counts it against them
as if they ate from offerings to the dead,
phrases.notes: 'The dead' is a way of referring to idols.

phrases.english: as it says: 'And he will call you, and you will eat of his sacrifice.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the case of a feast for a son, mentioned in the משנה (step 9) and the ברייתא (step 24). It adds a new point: the guests themselves are guilty.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Jews who go to a non-Jew's feast for his son are treated as if they ate idol offerings, even if they eat only their own food.

steps.title: Why not say the guilt begins only when they eat?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's reading. Maybe the פסוק blames them only once they actually eat from the sacrifice.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe we should say the guilt begins only once he actually eats!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא. It suggests that the פסוק only blames someone who actually eats from the idol's sacrifice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'and you will eat of his sacrifice'. That sounds like eating is what matters. If so, guests who eat only their own food should not be blamed at all, and רבי ישמעאל's point would fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: But say instead (a suggestion that pushes back)

phrases.english: But say: only once he actually eats!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the way step 27 read the פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ישמעאל's claim that the guests are guilty even without eating from the sacrifice
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק mentions eating from the sacrifice. That suggests the guilt depends on actually eating it, not just on being at the feast.

steps.title: רבא: the guilt starts from the moment of the invitation
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that if the guilt began only with eating, the פסוק would not need the words 'and he will call you'. Those extra words teach that the guilt begins from the invitation. The step ends with 'therefore', which leads into the next part.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If so, the פסוק should have just said 'and you will eat of his sacrifice'. Why does it add 'and he will call you'? To teach that the guilt starts from the moment of the invitation! Therefore...
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends the ברייתא by pointing to an extra phrase in the פסוק. He then begins a 'therefore' that sets up the practical rule in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'and he will call you' would be unnecessary if eating were the only issue. So they must teach something: being invited and taking part already brings the guilt. That supports רבי ישמעאל.

keyTerms.meaning: From the moment of the invitation

steps.whatToRemember: The phrase 'and he will call you' teaches that going to a non-Jew's celebration feast is a problem from the invitation itself, not only from eating.
steps.whyThisMatters: It moves the problem from what the guest eats to the fact that he takes part in the non-Jew's celebration.

phrases.english: Rava said: If so,
let the verse just say, 'and you will eat of his sacrifice.'
Why does it add 'and he will call you'?
To teach that it begins from the moment of the invitation!
Therefore,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: אִם כֵּן, נֵימָא קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the פסוק closely: an extra phrase shows when the guilt begins
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The guilt begins only when the guest actually eats from the sacrifice.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'And he will call you' shows that the guilt begins from the time of the invitation.
